```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
has_torch <- torch::torch_is_installed()
```

```{r setup}
library(graphlearnR)
```

Full batch training runs every layer on every node in every step. Memory then
grows with the whole graph. A model with $L$ layers only needs the
$L$ hop neighborhood of the nodes in the loss, so large graphs are trained on
sampled subgraphs around small batches of *seed* nodes, as in GraphSAGE
(Hamilton, Ying, and Leskovec 2017).

## Sampling a computation graph

`sample_neighbors()` starts at the seeds and, hop by hop, samples at most
`fanouts[h]` incoming edges of each frontier node. The result is an ordinary
`graph_data` with extra fields.

```{r}
g <- dataset_karate()
sg <- sample_neighbors(g, seeds = c(1, 34), fanouts = c(3, 2), seed = 1)
sg
sg$n_id
sg$hop
sg$num_seeds
```

* The seeds come first, in the order given, so `out[1:num_seeds, ]` are the
  predictions that enter the loss.
* `n_id` maps local node `i` back to the original node `n_id[i]`, and `e_id`
  does the same for edges.
* `hop` is the hop at which each node was first reached.

Mapping local edges back to original ids recovers edges of the input graph:

```{r}
local <- sg$edge_index[, 1:4]
rbind(from = sg$n_id[local[1, ]], to = sg$n_id[local[2, ]])
```

A fanout of `-1` keeps every neighbor. With full fanouts the sample is the
exact $L$ hop computation graph, so a model gives the same predictions on the
seeds as on the full graph. `k_hop_subgraph()` is the shortcut for that case.

```{r, eval = has_torch}
library(torch)
torch_manual_seed(1)
m <- gnn_model("sage", 34, 16, 2, num_layers = 2)
m$eval()
full <- as.array(graphlearnR:::model_forward(m, graph_tensors(g)))
sub <- k_hop_subgraph(g, c(1, 34), k = 2)
part <- as.array(graphlearnR:::model_forward(m, graph_tensors(sub)))
max(abs(part[1:2, ] - full[c(1, 34), ]))
```

## Loaders

`node_loader()` splits the seed nodes into batches and samples a subgraph
for each. Each epoch uses a different, reproducible shuffle and sample.

```{r}
g <- split_nodes(g, seed = 1)
ld <- node_loader(g, batch_size = 8, fanouts = c(5, 5), seed = 1)
ld
batches <- loader_batches(ld, epoch = 1)
vapply(batches, function(b) c(seeds = b$num_seeds, nodes = num_nodes(b)), numeric(2))
```

`graph_loader()` does the same for graph level datasets, yielding
`graph_batch` objects.

## Mini-batch training

Give `train_graph_model()` the `fanouts` and `batch_size` arguments and it
trains on sampled subgraphs. The loss is computed on seed nodes only;
sampled neighbors provide context but no gradient signal of their own.

```{r, eval = has_torch}
big <- split_nodes(dataset_sbm(c(300, 300, 300), p_in = 0.03, p_out = 0.002,
                               feature_signal = 0.5, seed = 2), seed = 2)
torch_manual_seed(2)
fit <- train_graph_model(gnn_model("sage", 8, 32, 3), big, "node_classification",
                         epochs = 15, fanouts = c(10, 5), batch_size = 128,
                         seed = 2)
fit
evaluate_graph_model(fit, big)
```

Prediction and evaluation run on the full graph, so the reported numbers do
not depend on the sampling.

## Subgraph batches: Cluster-GCN and GraphSAINT

Neighbor sampling grows each batch outward from seed nodes. Two other
strategies train on whole subgraphs instead, and plug into the same
trainer through the `loader` argument.

`cluster_loader()` follows Cluster-GCN: it partitions the graph once and
each batch is the subgraph induced by a few parts, edges between them
included. Parts follow Louvain communities, so most edges stay inside a
batch.

```{r, eval = has_torch}
cl <- cluster_loader(big, num_parts = 12, clusters_per_batch = 3, seed = 1)
cl
summary(lengths(cl$parts))
torch_manual_seed(2)
fit_cl <- train_graph_model(gnn_model("sage", 8, 32, 3), big, "node_classification",
                            epochs = 15, loader = cl, seed = 2)
evaluate_graph_model(fit_cl, big)
```

`saint_loader()` follows the GraphSAINT random walk sampler. Each batch is
the subgraph induced by the nodes that short random walks visit. Nodes and
edges are not sampled uniformly, so the loader estimates how often each one
appears and corrects for it: the loss of each node is weighted by
`node_norm` and edge weights are rescaled, as in PyTorch Geometric's
`GraphSAINTSampler`.

```{r, eval = has_torch}
sl <- saint_loader(big, batch_size = 100, walk_length = 2, num_steps = 8, seed = 1)
sl
b <- loader_batches(sl)[[1]]
c(nodes = num_nodes(b), edges = num_edges(b))
summary(b$node_norm)
torch_manual_seed(2)
fit_sl <- train_graph_model(gnn_model("sage", 8, 32, 3), big, "node_classification",
                            epochs = 15, loader = sl, seed = 2)
evaluate_graph_model(fit_sl, big)
```

Both loaders return `graph_data` batches whose `node_ids` hold the original
node indices, so a batch can be inspected like any other graph.

## Negative sampling

Link prediction needs pairs that are not edges. `negative_sampling()` draws
them by rejection, excluding the given positives, self loops (unless
allowed), and duplicates. For undirected graphs it returns canonical pairs
with `from < to` and excludes both directions of each positive. Bipartite
sampling draws sources and targets from different node sets.

```{r}
pos <- dataset_karate()$edge_index
neg <- negative_sampling(pos, num_nodes = 34, num_samples = 5, directed = FALSE,
                         seed = 1)
neg
negative_sampling(rbind(1:3, 1:3), num_src = 5, num_dst = 4, num_samples = 4,
                  seed = 1)
```

## Practical notes

* Throughput depends mostly on the number of sampled edges, which is about
  `batch_size * prod(fanouts)`. Start with fanouts like `c(10, 10)` and
  lower them if memory is tight.
* Sampling runs in R on the CPU. On graphs that fit in memory, full batch
  training is usually faster: on a GitHub runner, an 8,000 node graph took
  0.16 s per full batch epoch and 1.0 s per sampled epoch. Sample when the
  full graph does not fit.
* The model runs on whichever device you pass as `device`. For very large
  graphs, keep the graph in memory once and let the loader slice it, rather
  than building many graph copies.
* Memory: in one run on a GitHub Ubuntu runner (CPU only), the peak
  resident memory of a fresh R process for one forward and backward pass
  on a random graph with 50,000 nodes, 500,000 edges and 32 features was
  about 560 MB for `sage_conv`, 580 MB for `gin_conv`, 1.1 GB for
  `gcn_conv` and 1.3 GB for `gat_conv`, against about 290 MB after loading
  torch. GPU memory has not been measured.
* Construction: building an undirected graph with 1,000,000 input edges
  took 2.6 s in the same run, against 0.05 s for a directed one, so build
  large graphs once and reuse them.
* The `benchmarks/` folder of the source repository has timing scripts for
  layers and for full batch against sampled training. Their results are
  produced on GitHub Actions runners and reported with the hardware they ran
  on.
